land.text: Sichuan: Meng Zhixiang's Xichuan and Dongchuan circuits

predecessors.note: The infobox lists the Later Tang as the predecessor. Hanzhong (Shannan West) followed in the last days of Meng Zhixiang's reign in 934; the Qin/Feng/Cheng/Jie country did not come from the Later Tang: the Meng Chang page has it surrender to Later Shu from the Later Jin around the new year 947 (ledger).

successors.note: Infobox 'Surrendered to Song: 965'; the Song took Sichuan, but the four prefectures had been Later Zhou's since 955 and were Song land with the Later Zhou's succession in 960.

capitals.name: Chengdu
capitals.note: 'located in present-day Sichuan with its capital in Chengdu'; the infobox gives no capital years.

rulers.name: Gaozu (Meng Zhixiang)
rulers.note: Emperor of Later Shu from 16 March 934; died 7 September 934.

rulers.name: Houzhu (Meng Chang)
rulers.note: Infobox 'Reign: September 10, 934 - February 23, 965'; era names Mingde (934-938) and Guangzheng (938-965) (Later Shu page).

correction.text: Meng Zhixiang's Sichuan (proclaimed 16 March 934) with Hanzhong (Shannan West), which 'surrendered to Later Shu in the last days of Meng Zhixiang's reign', without the Qin/Feng/Cheng/Jie country: the Meng Chang page has the Xiongwu circuit and Feng surrender to Later Shu from the Later Jin only around the new year 947

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria starts the row in 936, although the Later Shu page gives 'Established: 934, in Chengdu' (the Five Dynasties page prints both 934-965 and 935-965). Repaired after review: the first draft used the whole 936 shape, which holds 30,854 km2 of the Qin/Feng/Cheng/Jie country (gazetteer cell count, my arithmetic) that was Later Tang and then Later Jin land until 947.

606,099 km2 in Cliopatria; the shape is the Former Shu outline (605,241 km2) and reaches 35.5 N. The Later Shu page gives no area and says only 'located in present-day Sichuan'; the Five Dynasties page says it 'basically controlled the same territory as its predecessor'. Repaired after review (verdict ok -> adjust): the Meng Chang page names Xichuan, Dongchuan, Shannan West (Hanzhong) and Wei Prefecture among Later Shu territories and dates the surrender of Xiongwu (Qin, Jie, Cheng) and Feng to around the new year 947, so the 936-946 years lose them. Before 947 the page has Later Shu fail against Jie and Cheng (944) and be 'repelled by an army launched from Later Jin's Qin Prefecture'.

correction.text: the 936 shape valid 936-946 without the Qin/Feng/Cheng/Jie country: the four prefectures were Later Tang and Later Jin land until the Xiongwu circuit and Feng surrendered to Later Shu around the new year 947
the shape unchanged but valid 947-954 only: it begins in the year the four prefectures came to Later Shu (around the new year 947); from 955 they are cut out (later-shu_955)

keyframe_review.note: 605,668 km2, 431 km2 smaller than the 936 shape and otherwise identical. The shape now agrees with the ledger: it starts when Qin, Jie, Cheng and Feng surrendered to Later Shu (around the new year 947). Under 'In 955' the Meng Chang page says Later Zhou 'was planning an invasion to recover Feng, Qin, Cheng, and Jie Prefectures'; Qin, Cheng and Jie surrendered and Feng fell after a siege. Cliopatria never removes them. region.text: the Xichuan and Dongchuan circuits around Chengdu

ledger.note: 16 March 934: Meng Zhixiang proclaims the Later Shu in Chengdu. Meng Zhixiang page: his infobox gives 16 March 934 for his accession as emperor of Later Shu, after absorbing Dongchuan in 932-933 and becoming Prince of Shu in spring 933; the Later Shu page: 'Established: 934, in Chengdu'.

region.text: Shannan West Circuit, headquartered at Hanzhong

ledger.note: Late 934 (September by the reign end): Hanzhong comes over to the Later Shu. Shannan West Circuit, headquartered at Hanzhong, 'had surrendered to Later Shu in the last days of Meng Zhixiang's reign'; the Meng Zhixiang page: its governor Zhang Qianzhao surrendered during Li Congke's rebellion, 'allowing Later Shu to take the region south of the Qinling Mountains'.

region.text: Feng, Qin, Cheng and Jie Prefectures (the page names them, not their places; read as the Tianshui and Longnan country)

ledger.note: Around the new year 947: Later Shu takes the Xiongwu circuit and Feng from the Later Jin as its emperor falls. 'Around the new year 947, with a major Khitan Liao dynasty invasion force ... approaching' Kaifeng, the Later Jin emperor Shi Chonggui surrendered to Liao; the Xiongwu governor He Chongjian 'surrendered his circuit (including Qin, Jie, and Cheng Prefectures) to Later Shu'; Later Shu forces then attacked Feng Prefecture and its defender Shi Fengjun, of Later Jin's imperial clan, surrendered it too. Earlier tries had failed: in 944 the defector Wang Junhuai offered to guide a Later Shu army against Jie and Cheng, and a later incursion was 'repelled by an army launched from Later Jin's Qin Prefecture'. The first draft of this dossier dated the transfer to 934 from the Later Tang (confidence 1, page silent); the page does not say so. 'Around the new year' makes month 1 a sort key; the places are read from the names.

region.text: Feng, Qin, Cheng and Jie Prefectures (the page names them, not their places; read as the Tianshui and Longnan country)

ledger.note: 955: Later Zhou takes Feng, Qin, Cheng and Jie. 'Han then abandoned Qin Prefecture and fled back to Chengdu'; 'Cheng and Jie also surrendered to Later Zhou'; 'Wang Jing subsequently captured Feng Prefecture as well after a siege'. The page puts the attack under 'In 955' and gives no season; Guo Rong returned captured Shu soldiers in 957 without a treaty. Later Shu had held the four prefectures since around the new year 947 (ledger).

region.text: the northern front: Wang Quanbin came via Feng, bypassed Jianmen Pass, defeated Wang Zhaoyuan and reached Chengdu

ledger.note: 8 December 964: the Song invade the Later Shu on two fronts. The Song conquest of Later Shu page's infobox runs 'December 8, 964 - February 11, 965'; the Meng Chang page (second page): 'In 964, the Song emperor was planning to launch a major campaign to destroy Northern Han. Shortly after, he launched 60,000 men to attack on two fronts' (Wang Quanbin from Feng, Liu Guangyi from Gui Prefecture, which had been Song since 963), without a month or an order of the fronts. The Wang Quanbin page did not load.

region.text: the northern front: Wang Quanbin came via Feng, bypassed Jianmen Pass, defeated Wang Zhaoyuan and reached Chengdu

ledger.note: 11 February 965: the fighting ends with the surrender at Chengdu. The Song conquest of Later Shu page's infobox ends the war on 11 February 965 and says Meng Chang 'surrendered within 70 days' of the invasion; the Meng Chang page (second page): 'When Wang Quanbin reached Chengdu, Meng surrendered to him, ending Later Shu', with the infobox reign ending 23 February 965 (the loss and dissolve below keep 23 February; the two infoboxes differ by twelve days).

ledger.note: 23 February 965: the whole Later Shu realm passes to the Song. Infobox 'Reign: September 10, 934 - February 23, 965'; the Later Shu page: 'Surrendered to Song: 965'. Meng Chang went to Kaifeng in spring 965 and died there.

region.text: the Later Shu without the four prefectures Later Zhou took in 955

ledger.note: February 965: the Later Shu ends. Infobox 'Surrendered to Song: 965'; Five Dynasties page: 'The kingdom was ruled well until forced to succumb to Song armies in 965' and 'Jingnan and Wuping Jiedushi were swept away in 963, Later Shu in 965.' The February month is the Meng Chang infobox's reign end.

wars.name: Later Shu seizure of Xiongwu and Feng

zones.text: Feng, Qin, Cheng and Jie Prefectures (the page names them, not their places; read as the Tianshui and Longnan country)

wars.outcome: As the Later Jin emperor surrendered to the Liao around the new year 947, the Xiongwu governor He Chongjian surrendered his circuit (Qin, Jie, Cheng) to Later Shu and, after Later Shu forces attacked Feng Prefecture, Shi Fengjun surrendered it too.
wars.note: Earlier failed tries: Wang Junhuai's defection in 944 (offering to guide a Later Shu army to Jie and Cheng) and a later incursion repelled from Qin Prefecture, undated beyond 'subsequent'. The places are read from the names.

wars.name: Later Shu aid to the Guanzhong rebels against Later Han

zones.text: Fengxiang, where Wang Jingchong was sent 'toward Jinchang and Fengxiang to prepare to combat the Later Shu troops' (read as the Baoji country)

wars.outcome: Later Shu 'launched troops to try to aid Wang and Zhao Siwan' against Later Han, but the army was 'initially repelled by the Later Han general Zhao Hui'; Wang Jingchong killed himself. No land changed hands on the page.
wars.note: The page gives no year for any of the Guanzhong events (checked by asking for each): they follow its 'Around the new year 947' passage, so 947 is the order's reading and the war may run later; the later-han dossier should date the rebellions. Fengxiang is read as the Baoji country.

wars.name: Later Zhou campaign against Later Shu

zones.text: Feng, Qin, Cheng and Jie Prefectures (the page names them, not their places; read as the Tianshui and Longnan country)

wars.outcome: Later Zhou took Qin, Cheng, Jie and Feng Prefectures; Meng Chang asked for peace as 'Emperor of the Great Shu' and got no answer; Guo Rong returned several thousand captured soldiers in 957.
wars.note: The page puts the whole campaign under 'In 955'; the siege of Feng may have run into 956 (page silent). Emissaries sent to Northern Han and Southern Tang seeking alliances in 955: both agreed but did not act.

wars.name: Song conquest of Later Shu

zones.text: the northern front: Wang Quanbin came via Feng, bypassed Jianmen Pass, defeated Wang Zhaoyuan and reached Chengdu

wars.outcome: Song armies under Wang Quanbin (north, via Feng) and Liu Guangyi (east, from Gui Prefecture) overran the Shu; Meng Chang surrendered at Chengdu in early 965.
wars.note: A secret letter to the Northern Han proposing simultaneous strikes on the Song was betrayed by a messenger in 964. The Song conquest of Later Shu page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_conquest_of_Later_Shu) dates the war 8 December 964 to 11 February 965 and gives no route or order of the fronts; the Wang Quanbin page did not load.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey fixes any Later Shu border; the Qinling frontier with the Later Zhou from 955 follows the prefectures Later Zhou took, and the western and southern edges (Tibetans, Dali) are approximate.

notes:
Later Shu (Cliopatria 936-969, 3 shapes). Cliopatria starts the row two years late (state 934) and runs it four years past the end (surrendered February 965); its 947 and 962 shapes are the 936 outline with a 431 km2 trim and never lose the four prefectures Later Zhou took in 955.

Page budget: 4 pages opened in the first pass (two shared with other states of this batch) and 1 more in the repair pass (Song conquest of Later Shu); the Later Shu article is a stub. Settled in the repair pass: the Qin/Feng/Cheng/Jie country came to the Shu around the new year 947 from the Later Jin (He Chongjian's and Shi Fengjun's surrenders, Meng Chang page), not in 934 from the Later Tang; the Song invasion began 8 December 964 (Song conquest page). Not settled: the prefectures the Song took first (neither page says; the Wang Quanbin page did not load); the 955 lost land's exact places (read from names, not on the pages); what Later Shu held in 956-964 beyond the four prefectures. Date conflicts: the Song conquest page ends the war on 11 February 965, the Meng Chang infobox ends the reign on 23 February 965; Five Dynasties page prints both 934-965 and 935-965 for the Later Shu; Meng Chang infobox reign start 10 September 934 and Meng Zhixiang's death 7 September 934 (Meng Zhixiang page); the Meng Chang prose puts the surrender at Chengdu without a date while the infobox ends the reign on 23 February 965.

Mirrors wanted: later-tang (loss of Sichuan 16 March 934, vassal 933-934; already there), later-jin (loss of the four prefectures around the new year 947; note that Cliopatria's Later Jin 936 shape holds only 9,610 km2 of them, 30,854 km2 lying in the Later Shu 936 shape), later-zhou (gain of the four prefectures 955), northern-song (gain 965 and the 964 contest). Dali (kingdom-of-dali) is a neighbour from 947 with no event on the pages opened.
